name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47

voice.register: Fast, warm and run-on: a man walking between two building sites with his right arm up, talking to someone far away. His shape is the job that grows and the worry that stacks. Inside one bubble he chains clauses with commas, and the 'ek kaam' he started with becomes three ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'); his questions are worry checks about named people, stacked, and he waits only for the answer to the last one, 'Pakka?'. A long thought runs on into a second or third bubble, picked up with 'aur' or, once a scene at most, 'aur haan'. Every bubble still ends cleanly, on a full stop, a question mark or a '!', so on a phone nothing looks cut off. That is what tells his long runs from the other three: Papa's are whole sentences in order with the times in them, Masterji's a verdict and a wander, Mausi's a tripled word and a question she answers herself; his is a list that keeps growing and a stack he waits on, and he never answers his own question. The common fillers (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, bas, theek hai) come into his talk the way they come into anyone's; what marks him is the shape and where his words come from: people, health and city logistics. Feeling is said out loud, warmly, to one person at a time, with a hug: he is one of the two elders who say it in plain words (Mausi says hers to the whole room, loud; he says his to one face). Fear he says only to Mami. Humour is big and kind and aimed at himself (he plans nothing, he talks too much, he cannot say no to sweets), never at anyone's age, town, shop or work. He talks most to people far away, Mummy first ('Didi!'); in chapter 5, with the phone in his pocket, to everyone at the gate. With Nani alone he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows for, and lets her finish before he speaks. When cross he does not go quiet or slow (that is Mami's tell in his chapter): he still asks after the other man's family first, then the run-on stops dead and breaks into single words, one downward chop of his free hand on each ('Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.'). Never at family, a woman, a worker's dignity or anyone on a card. When anyone brings a report of harassment or a dowry demand he believes it at once and moves ('Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.'), with no 'Pakka?' and no question back (rule 22). His voice is never raised except the chapter's one shout at 5.03 (rule 35). Warm, and never the comic one while he is the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: The most English elder. Hinglish: a whole English clause first, at speed, then a Hindi landing ('Don't worry, Bade Jija ji ko bulao.'). His English carries the jobs and the comfort (don't worry, no problem, sorted, last minute, booking, advance, I'll miss you), and his Hindi lands on family, food and health (Amma, Didi, ghar, sab, khaana, dawai, man, roz). Like most city people under fifty he also builds everyday verbs from an English word with kar or ho, and his are people and logistics verbs: 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. Mummy's English verbs are the shop counter turned on home things ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), so the two stay apart by what they turn into verbs, not by who may use the pattern. Mami, the other whole-clause switcher, runs the other way: a Hindi clause, then an English status. 'Ek kaam karo' to you, Tinku and Mami; 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders. Everyday Urdu-rooted words are his too, as they are the whole town's: 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor', 'ain waqt'. Figures in Hinglish bubbles are digits ('60? 70 kar do!'), because romanised 'saath' is also 'with'. He cheers good news by making it bigger, not with 'Badhai ho' or 'Congratulations', which go to Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, so he does not echo them in a shared panel. HINDI MODE: everyday spoken city Hindi in Devanagari that keeps the English loan words a Hindi-first reader already knows (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, लिस्ट, वेटिंग, डिपार्टमेंट, क्रेडिट), so he still sorts in Hindi; where his Hinglish has a whole English phrase, Hindi mode uses the Hindi a Devanagari speaker would say ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), never English spelled out in Devanagari; 'चिंता मत करो', 'चिंता नहीं' or 'फ़िक्र मत कीजिए' for 'don't worry'; with Nani, whole Hindi sentences and आप. ENGLISH MODE: plain British English with his rhythm; 'oh, and' for 'aur haan'; 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter (his one Indian-English turn), otherwise 'One small job'; 'Oho!' stays; kin words stay as they are (Didi, Jija ji, Amma, Boss); never a spelled accent and never a word-for-word line ('everyone must come', not 'everyone comes').
tics: The job that grows: 'Ek kaam karo,' and the one job becomes two or three in the same comma chain ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'). The 'ek' is an idiom, not a count. 'Aur haan' (English mode 'oh, and') carries the run into one more bubble at most once a scene; every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', never on a trailing comma.

Stacks worry questions about named people and waits only for the last answer: 'Amma ka BP check hua? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?'. He never answers his own question (Mausi's shape) and never asks how you are (Nani's 'Aur tum.' closes that in the album). Each person in the stack gets a verb or a noun with them ('Amma ka BP check hua?', 'Amma andar hain?'), never a bare kin word. To you, Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy' ('Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?'), because 'Didi, kaisi hain?' said aloud, or with a comma, is him calling you Didi, and कैसी then gives you a gender.
Ends a worry stack, or a reassurance he is given, with 'Pakka?' ('Sure?'); at 5.27 it turns round into a statement. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).

People first, then business: every vendor gets 'Ghar mein sab theek?' and a question about their own people (a mother's knee, the children's exams) before 'Achha.' and the job. Names, not numbers, are his stock, and he keeps it even when cross ('Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.').

Makes everything bigger in words, never in figures: aur, sab, sabko, extra, poora, 'phir aur upar, phir sabse upar'. 'Full' ('full fit') in at most two lines a chapter; the rest of the time 'poora'. The plus-ten is a gesture, the flashed open hand, with no figure said; the only spoken figures in his year are 5.03 and 5.27.
Hands the how to someone else in the same breath: 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao.', 'Credit Jija ji ka.'. He plans nothing; he knows who can.

Credits people out loud by their job, to whoever is near: 'In-charge se miliye!', 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' (Papa the parcel clerk, promoted in words), and from December 'District scorer se miliye!' (outside any decision beat, guests off the panel).
'Oho!' for good or bad news, by tone: rising with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at bad news. 'Aaiye' once at the gate, never three times.
Never talks over Nani: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back.
Hugs everyone he can reach while he says it out loud (a stage direction, never a word). Never you: household hands never reach towards you (rule 7).
catchphrases: 'Ek kaam karo, ...' | 'एक काम करो, ...' | 'Do one thing, ...' The one job that becomes three before the full stop. 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders; in English mode 'Do one thing' once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job,'.
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' The end of every worry stack. Turned round once, at 5.27: 'Pakka.' | 'पक्का।' | 'For sure.' Never said after a report (rule 22).

'60? 70 kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' His quoted line and his only catchphrase with a number, said once, at 5.03, the chapter's one shout, with the open hand flashed. The owner is asked whether to keep both marked figures (matrix open point).
voice.exclamation: 'Oho!' | 'ओहो!' | 'Oho!' (the same in every mode). For good news and bad, and the tone tells which: a rising 'Oho!' with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at a delay or a worry. It is a sound with no word in it, so it has no religious sense, and no one else in the cast has it as their exclamation. Guard: never run on into a god-word, and never the city man's reflexes 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Shukar hai' or 'Bhagwan ka shukar' (rule 3). Each person keeps one exclamation of their own, so he does not use the others' ('Kamaal hai.' Papa, 'Arre waah.' Captain sahab, 'Haaye!' Mausi, 'Had hai!' Mummy, 'Baap re.' Nani, 'Hain?' Mausa ji, 'Uff.' Masterji, 'Gazab!' Tinku, 'Ish.' Mami, 'Badhiya.' you). A plain 'arre' in the middle of a line is free, as it is for anyone. Thanked, he opens on his own sound, 'Oho, no no!', not on Mummy's 'Arre, isme kya'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: in plain words, out loud, then the blame made bigger: 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' | 'सॉरी, दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा।' | 'Sorry, Didi, it's all my fault.'. Said to whoever he let down, in front of everyone, and to the next person in the same breath ('Jija ji, aapse bhi sorry. Aapki neend kharab ki.'); to you the same, plainly ('Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'). Mausi's sorry is the tripled 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with food held out; his is one 'sorry' and the whole blame. THANKS: a plain 'Thank you' to anyone who helped, with a word for their people: 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.' | 'थैंक यू, [नाम] भाई! माँ जी का ख़याल रखिए।' | 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Look after your mother.'. For family, the thank-you is the room hearing what they did: 'In-charge se miliye!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the one in charge!'; for Papa 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' | 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर से मिलिए!' | 'Meet our very own station master!'. Thanked himself, he brushes it off with his own exclamation and gives it away: 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' ('Arre, isme kya' is Mummy's brush-off, so he does not echo it). To Mami in private, a plain 'Thank you' after what she did, said back to her. LOVE: said in plain words, one to one, with a hug: 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.'; at a parting 'Didi, I'll miss you.' | 'दीदी, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगेगा।' and the worry stack after it; to Mami in private, what she did said back to her ('Aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha. Thank you.'). Mausi's love is 'Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.' to the room; his is 'bahut miss kiya' to one face. 'Bahut' is the commonest word in the language and free to both; the phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' is hers, and his Hindi mode keeps 'एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा', not her 'बहुत याद आई'. FEAR: only to Mami ('Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.').

'Don't worry' | 'चिंता मत करो' / 'चिंता नहीं' / 'फ़िक्र मत कीजिए' | 'Don't worry' (to others, never about himself)
'No problem' | 'नो प्रॉब्लम' | 'No problem' (comfort)
'Achha.' | 'अच्छा।' | 'Right.' or 'Good.' (the hinge from people to the job)
'sorted' | 'सेट' | 'sorted' (the word he wants back from you)

'Ghar mein sab theek?' | 'घर में सब ठीक?' | 'All well at home?' (to every vendor, before business)

People and logistics verbs with kar or ho: 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye' | 'मन नहीं लगा', 'फ़ोन करो', 'बुक कर दीजिए', 'चेक हुआ', 'भेज दीजिए' | 'missed', 'ring', 'book', 'checked', 'send'
'Sorry' | 'सॉरी' | 'Sorry' (once, then the blame); 'Thank you' | 'थैंक यू' | 'Thank you' (to whoever helped)
'Oho, no no!' | 'ओहो, ना ना!' | 'Oho, no no!' (when he is thanked, before he gives the credit away)
'credit' | 'क्रेडिट' | 'credit' (always given away; the same loan in Hindi mode, so the Hindi line says what the Hinglish says)
'[job] se miliye!' | '[जॉब] से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the [job]!'
'department' | 'डिपार्टमेंट' | 'department' (his joke at himself: plans are Boss's department)
'arrangement' | 'इंतज़ाम' | 'arrangements'; 'last minute' | 'ऐन वक़्त पर' | 'at the last minute'; 'advance' | 'एडवांस' | 'advance' (5.06)
'bahut miss kiya' | 'एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा' | 'missed you so much' (his love line)
'Aaiye' | 'आइए' | 'Come in' (guests, once); 'zaroor aaiye' | 'ज़रूर आइए' | 'do come' (his invitation)
'Oho' | 'ओहो' | 'Oho'
Common fillers in the middle of a line, as anyone uses them: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, bas, theek hai.
Trade words, only outside chapter 5: pressure, flow, site, order, dispatch, pump.
never: Any spoken figure but the two marked beats (5.03 '60? 70 kar do!', 5.27 '60 plates. Pakka.'): no counts, times, prices, ages, 'do din', '60 kursiyaan'; no ordinals, not even 'first job' or 'first class'. The idiom 'ek kaam' is not a count.
A number smaller than his last, or 'kam karo' | 'कम करो' | 'cut it', in public. The one exception is 5.27.
'Nahi' to a guest; 'pata nahi' | 'पता नहीं' | 'I don't know'; 'baad mein dekhenge' | 'बाद में देखेंगे' | 'we'll see later'.

Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22): never 'Pakka?', 'Sach mein?' or any question back after one; he says 'Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' and moves. No proof words ('saboot', 'likhit', 'proof', 'in writing') anywhere near a report beat.
A bubble that ends on a trailing comma, or more than one 'aur haan' in a scene: on a phone it reads as a bubble cut off, and on every line it turns into a tag.
'Full' in more than two lines a chapter (it becomes the slangy-uncle gimmick); 'poora' does the rest.

Other people's set phrases (owners keep phrases, not fillers): 'Hmm. Ho jayega.', 'So jao.', 'Lo. Aadha.', 'Galti hui.', 'Mazboot.' and a one-word 'Theek.' or 'Lo.' line (Mausa ji); 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Chai piyo.', 'Dandi mat maarna.', 'Sab aayein.' (Nani); 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'Maine kaha tha na?' (Mausi); 'Haan ji, boliye.', 'Ye mere hisaab mein.', 'Iska bill nahin.' (Mummy); '9:40, aaspaas nahin.', 'Chart ban chuka hai.' (Papa); 'Straight bat. Front foot.', 'Next ball.', 'Dead ball', 'Not out' (Captain sahab); the readback ending 'Correct?' and the status pair 'pending' / 'done', 'Mera item tha.' (Mami); 'Bas abhi.', 'Barabar.' (Masterji); 'Kitaab mein.', 'Faisla tumhara.' (Tinku); 'Pehle ___.', 'Maaf kijiye.', 'Sab set.', 'Dikhaiye.' (yours). Single common words are not owned: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free mid-line.

Other people's shapes: answering his own question or tripling a word (Mausi); the number before the noun (Papa, Tinku); items as 'thing, status' (Mami); closed verbless fragments outside his cross beat (Nani, Mausa ji); tea as his care (Nani's sorry, Masterji's love); a sugar joke about the tea itself (Nani and Papa have one).

Religious words and exclamations (rule 3): 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Hai Ram', 'Bhagwan', 'Shukar hai', 'Inshallah', 'Mashallah', 'Rab', 'Wahe Guru', 'Jesus'; in English mode also 'Gosh', 'Good Lord', 'Thank goodness', 'Thank heavens', 'Heavens'.
'Main hoon na' as a line of comfort: in his mouth it is heard as the film, so his comfort is 'Don't worry' and a job handed on.
Dowry or ritual words: 'dahej' | 'दहेज', 'lena-dena' | 'लेन-देन', 'kanyadaan', 'vidaai', 'phere', 'mandap', 'shagun', 'baraat'; nothing at all about gifts for the groom's side (rules 22 and 27).
His daughter's name or looks, or 'giving her away'.
'Chhota shehar' | 'छोटा शहर' | 'small town', or any put-down of Nani's town, Mummy's shop or Papa's punctuality; no age joke.

In chapter 5 bubbles (rule 36): 'phone' | 'फ़ोन' or 'call' | 'कॉल' anywhere in the chapter; 'pump' | 'पंप', 'motor' | 'मोटर', 'generator' | 'जनरेटर'; 'gate lights' before 5.07; 'old folks' or 'old ways' before 5.15 and 5.24.

To you: any word that gives you a gender ('beta' | 'बेटा', 'bhanja' | 'भांजा', 'bhanji' | 'भांजी', 'bachcha' | 'बच्चा', 'bhai', 'champ', 'yaar', 'hero'); a kin word standing alone in a bubble to you, or 'Didi' before a verb that agrees with a person ('Didi?' and 'Didi kaisi hain?' read, aloud or with a comma, as calling you Didi, and कैसी then gives you a gender; to you Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy', or 'Mummy' in a possessive such as 'Mummy ki dukaan'); and any Hindi that fails rule 66: 'तुम आ गए?', 'थक गए?', 'करोगे?', 'हमारे इंचार्ज', a participle before रहो, रहना or रहिए ('खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो', 'खाते रहो'), or a 'we' that takes you in with a gendered verb ('हम देखते हैं').
Brands of any kind: no phone, car, pump or sweet-shop name (rule 3).
address: NANI: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा'; आप and -इए ('Amma, aap baithiye.'). Short whole sentences; he lets her finish and repeats her last two words. She calls him 'छोटे'.
MUMMY: 'Didi' | 'दीदी'; आप, softened with 'na' ('Didi, rakh lijiye na.'). The first person he rings about anything. She calls him 'Chhote' ('Chhote ji' with आप when she is angry).

PAPA: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी'; आप. To guests, 'Ghar ke station master' | 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर' | 'our very own station master': the parcel clerk promoted in words. Papa's word for him is for the family address table.
MAUSI: 'Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी' (plain 'Didi' is Mummy); आप. She calls him 'Munna', तुम.
MAUSA JI: 'Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी'; आप. He calls him 'Chhote', तुम.
TINKU: 'Tinku'; तुम ('Tinku, ek kaam karo.'). To guests 'our youngest' until December, then 'District scorer se miliye!'. She says 'Mama ji' and आप.
MAMI: 'Boss' | 'बॉस', in front of the family and in private; तुम both ways. Her name is never said on screen; she calls him no name, and 'your Mama ji' to the young ones.
MASTERJI: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी'; आप. CAPTAIN SAHAB: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब'; आप (he greets him 'Catch?').
VENDORS he knows: first name with 'bhai' ('[name] bhai'), आप and -इए ('Ek kaam kijiye'); strangers and guests: 'Bhai sahab', 'Behen ji', 'Aaiye'; आप to all, even when cross.

YOU: तुम, only in rule 66 shapes: commands ('Ek kaam karo', 'gate pe raho', 'batao', 'sambhalo'), 'who should' asks ('Gate pe kaun rahe?' | 'गेट पर कौन रहे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('Sab tumhare bharose.', where तुम्हारे agrees with भरोसे). To others he names you by your job with no possessive that could agree with you ('In-charge se miliye!', 'Poora week inhone chalaya', never 'हमारे इंचार्ज'); a message to you opens 'In-charge!!'; his sorry to you is 'Sorry, In-charge'. In a bubble to you Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy' ('Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?') or 'Mummy' ('Mummy ki dukaan theek?'), as an uncle says to the child of the house; 'Didi' never comes alone and never before a verb that agrees with a person. No family word for you while rulebook Q7 is open. Your replies: 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' with आप.

Rule 66 checker flags on his lines to or around you, each for a native reader to clear: 'पक्का?' and 'अच्छा।' (words that never change); 'सब तुम्हारे भरोसे।' (भरोसे agrees with भरोसा); 'सबको जगह मिलनी चाहिए।' (agrees with जगह); 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' (तुम्हारी and कैसी agree with मम्मी); 'अम्मा अंदर हैं?'; 'पंप भेज रहा हूँ' (about himself); 'नौकरी लगी?' and 'अम्मा ने दवाई ली?' (they agree with नौकरी and दवाई); 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया।' (a ने past that agrees with हफ़्ता; but you are the doer, and rule 66 allows तुम-lines only as commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer, so this line waits on the owner adding 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape, or on the native reader clearing it onto the build's cleared list; no wording change is needed if the owner agrees).
All of these go into the one family address table the India review asks for, signed off by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (rule 65).
samples: ORDER, the job that grows, to you, ch 5 at Nani's gate, outside any decision beat (commands and a 'who should' shape only, rule 66). EN: 'Do one thing, take the gate, bring everyone in.' / 'Oh, and fetch Bade Jija ji, and get the chairs out.' / 'A seat for everyone. Sure?' | HINGLISH: 'Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.' / 'Aur haan, Bade Jija ji ko bulao, chairs bhi nikalwao.' / 'Sabko jagah milni chahiye. Pakka?' | HI: 'एक काम करो, गेट पर रहो, सबको अंदर लो।' / 'और हाँ, बड़े जीजा जी को बुलाओ, कुर्सियाँ भी निकलवाओ।' / 'सबको जगह मिलनी चाहिए। पक्का?'

WORRYING, to Mummy by phone from the city (the opening, or the writers' ear); the stack waits only for the last answer. EN: 'Didi! habits: Device: a big plain black phone in a thick black rubber case with one corner cracked on a site, painted with the screen dark and no logo, every word live text laid on top (rule 30). In chapter 5 it stays in his trouser pocket: never painted, never typed on screen.

Script: English and Roman Hinglish, never Devanagari (Nani's voice-typed Devanagari is the contrast). In the game's Hindi mode his messages show in Devanagari and keep his bursts and marks; where his Hinglish types a whole English phrase ('so proud', 'miss you all'), Hindi mode shows the Hindi a Devanagari typist would use ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), and single loans he would say anyway stay (बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग, प्लीज़).
Shape: the run-on typed as a burst. Four or five short messages, each one clause of it, 'aur haan' a message of its own at most once a burst, then 'calling' before you can reply.

The first message is the person's name, capitalised, with his doubled mark ('Didi!!', 'Jija ji!!', 'In-charge!!', '[Name] bhai!!'); everything after it is lowercase, kin names included ('amma', 'nani', 'chhote'), with no full stops. To Mami in private the name comes with no mark at all ('Boss').
Marks: '!!' is his; a worry question takes one '?', because '??' is Mausi's; never '!!!'.

Numbers: his bigness is typed in words (sab, everyone, extra), never as figures and never as the plus-ten. A digit appears only when a fact someone must act on cannot be said another way, and then he would rather ring.

Emoji: 🎉 for good news, ‼️ for worry, and 🤗 (a face with no person, gender or skin tone) for love typed in words ('miss you all 🤗'): he is the only one in the family who types love. Never a person emoji; no folded hands until the owner rules (realism notes).
Capitals once a year, for joy (Tinku's course letter), never in anger: all caps reads as shouting, the 'aggro uncle' trap (realism notes).

Voice notes from the back of an auto between sites, starting mid-word because he presses record late; shown as a voice-note strip with their words as live text, and they run on like his speech ('...aur haan, ek kaam aur,').

Forwards: only weather warnings for Nani's district, each with one line of his own ('amma ko andar rakhiye na!!'), the warning painted blank. Never politics, religion, gods, famous faces or false news (rule 3; caricature traps).

When: just before his eight o'clock call to Nani, at red lights, and late at night after Mami's list. He replies in seconds or not at all, because he rings instead, and never reads a long message to the end ('ok ok call me').

Short forms: 'pls', 'ok ok', 'msg'. English verbs with kar come into his typing as into his talk ('book kar dijiye pls'); 'ok ok call me' stays as it is, because the readers marked it true. No spelled accent and no typo played for laughs.
Thanks and sorry are typed plainly too ('thank you', 'sorry didi'), never as a code.
In private with Mami, and only there, his asks come down, in words: 'sabko?' becomes 'ok sab nahi' becomes 'tumhari list'.
The game has no group chat (owner, 23 Oct). On screen he is single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card under a panel, and a message on the player's own phone waits on rulebook Q9.

changed: COMMON FILLERS FREED (cast-wide 1): the never list no longer takes common words from him or gives them away. Arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free in the middle of a line; only set phrases stay with their owners ('Arre waah.', 'Kamaal hai.', 'Suno, suno, suno!', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, and the rest listed). 'Achha' and 'Pakka' are no longer his alone; what stays his is the place they sit: 'Achha.' as the hinge from people to the job, 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry stack.

THE SHAPE, NOT A TAG (real India 1): 'aur haan' now comes at most once a scene and every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', so nothing looks cut off on a phone. In the test set 'aur haan' is in 1 line of 12 (it was 8) and no bubble ends on a comma. His long run now shows inside one bubble as the job that grows ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.') and the worry stack that waits on 'Pakka?', which still reads apart from Papa's ordered sentences, Masterji's wander and Mausi's triple.

ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR OR HO ALLOWED (cast-wide 2): 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. He is told apart from Mummy by what he turns into a verb (people and logistics) against hers (home things in counter English). 'ok ok call me' is kept as it was, because the readers marked it true.

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3): sorry is a plain 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' and, to you, 'Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'; thanks is a plain 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.', a 'Thank you' to Mami in private, and when he is thanked his own brush-off, 'Oho, no no!', before the credit is given away (it was 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment). Credit by job stays for family, as his way of letting the room hear it, not as a trade code.

CONGRATULATIONS (cast-wide 4): 'Badhaai ho' is off his never list (rule 3 does not bar everyday phrases); it and 'Congratulations' are left for Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, and he cheers by making the news bigger ('Ab promotion, phir aur upar, phir sabse upar!').

RULE 22 GUARD ADDED (Hindi and rules note 2, cast-wide 5): never 'Pakka?', 'Sach mein?' or any question back after a report of harassment or a dowry demand, and no proof words near a report beat. A believe-first sample is added: 'Didi, main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' / 'Aap unke saath rahiye.' The register says it too.

LOVE LINE (real India 2): 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' became 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.', as a city son says it. 'Roz' was bending the line only because 'bahut' had been given to Mausi; 'bahut' is the commonest word in the language and is his again, while Mausi keeps her phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' (the matrix strike of his 'Bahut' is undone for this line). Typed love in Hinglish became 'chhote roz miss karta hai'.
RUMOUR LINE (real India 3): moment 8 is now 'Oho. Band? Mithai wale bhai theek toh hain? Pakka?', a reaction first and the shopkeeper himself, not a jump to his mother.

'FULL' CUT DOWN (real India 5): 'full' is in one test line ('Full fit!') and at most two lines a chapter; the sorry is 'poora kasoor', the tea is no longer 'full meethi', the gate order no longer says 'full'.

LONE KIN WORD TO YOU FIXED (Hindi and rules note 1): moment 10's bare 'Didi?' became 'Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' | 'How's your Mummy?' (9 counted words). 'Didi kaisi hain?' was tried first, but said aloud, or with a comma, it is him calling you Didi, and the feminine कैसी gives you a gender. The tics, never list and address table now bar a kin word alone, or 'Didi' before a verb that agrees with a person, in a bubble to you; 'Didi ki dukaan' in moment 9 is a possessive and stays (later mended to 'Mummy ki dukaan': to the child of the house an uncle says 'Mummy', as moment 10 does).

HINDI MODE TYPING (Hindi and rules note 3): 'सो प्राउड 🤗' became 'बहुत गर्व है 🤗' and 'मिस यू ऑल 🤗' became 'सबकी याद आती है 🤗'; Hinglish keeps 'so proud' and 'miss you all'. The mix now says Hindi mode never spells a whole English phrase in Devanagari.
टिकट ONE GENDER (Hindi and rules note 4): the Papa tease is now 'अगले साल का टिकट भी बुक कर लिया? / मेरा भी कर दीजिए।', masculine like Papa's file, so it cannot read as a slip.

ENGLISH MODE DE-TRANSLATED (cast-wide 10, real India 4): 'everyone comes!!' became 'everyone must come!!' (Hinglish 'sabko aana hai!!'); 'Meet the family's railway!' became 'Meet our very own station master!' (Hindi 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', which also settles the open question on the gender of रेलवे, and promotes the parcel clerk in words, his habit of making things bigger); 'Meet the in-charge!' became 'Meet the one in charge!'; the chairs joke reads 'Short of chairs? People stand, dinner's over sooner.'; 'All on you.' became 'It's all in your hands.'.

HINDI MODE FOR LOW-ENGLISH READERS (cast-wide 11): he keeps the loans most readers know (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग) but Hindi mode says 'भेज दीजिए' for 'dispatch'. 'Credit' stays क्रेडिट in Hindi mode, a loan the Hindi reader knows, because 'सारा काम' made the Hindi drift from the Hinglish.

SHARED BITS SPLIT (cast-wide 6): moment 11's 'Paani hi tha', one of four 'only water' lines, became 'Lagi toh nahi?', his worry going to the child; moment 4 no longer jokes about the sugar in the tea (Nani and Papa share that joke) but at himself ('Boss ko mat bataiye').
URDU-ROOTED WORDS SHARED (cast-wide 8): he now says 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor' and 'ain waqt' as everyday town words; a new inviting sample carries the first two.
VERBS BACK IN (cast-wide 9): his comfort and worry lines keep 'hai' and 'hoon' ('Amma andar hain?', 'Pump bhej raha hoon', 'Sabko jagah milni chahiye').

RULE 66 FLAG (cast-wide 0): the never list now bars any participle before रहो, रहना or रहिए ('खाते रहो' as well as 'खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो') and a 'we' that takes you in with a gendered verb; the credit line about you is a ने past ('इन्होंने चलाया').
WARMTH ADDED: a plain thank-you to Mami after what she held together, a word for the cook's mother after the thank-you, the invitation that asks for everyone, and a sorry to Papa for his lost sleep.

KEPT AS THE READERS MARKED IT TRUE: 'Pakka?'; 'Oho!'; 'Boss' for his wife; 'Ghar mein sab theek? Maa ji ka ghutna?' to every vendor; 'Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.' word for word; the chairs joke, now with the verb it was missing ('Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!'); 'Didi!!', 'ok ok call me' and 'DISTRICT LEVEL!! 🎉🎉'. Also kept: his essence, want, fear and contradiction (worries about everything, plans nothing; makes anyone come); 'Ek kaam karo'; the stacked worry questions he never answers himself; people before business; the cross tell; slowing only for Nani; fear said only to Mami; the two marked figures; the address table.

CHAIRS JOKE MENDED (Hindi and rules): 'log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega' had no verb after 'khade-khade' and read as broken Hindi, not as his run-on. It is now 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!' | 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े खाएँगे। जल्दी निपटेगा!' (9 words); the future agrees with लोग, not with you.

THANKED, HIS OWN SOUND (Hindi and rules): moment 7 opened on 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment, and its Hindi said 'सारा काम' where the Hinglish said 'Credit'. It is now 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' (8 words).

'JUST CHECKING IN' OUT (real India): it is American office English. The worry call to Mummy now opens 'Haan, Didi! Bas aise hi phone kiya, kuch khaas nahi.', as the Hindi mode already had it; English mode 'Didi! Just thought I'd ring, nothing special.'

RULE 66, THE ने PAST (cast-wide): 'Poora week inhone chalaya' | 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया' marks no gender, since the verb agrees with हफ़्ता, but you are the doer, and rule 66 names only three shapes. No wording change; it waits on the owner (see OPEN).

OPEN, for the owner and readers: may rule 66 add a fourth shape, 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' (here 'Poora week inhone chalaya'; the same shape sits in Tinku's, Mausi's, Papa's and Mummy's files), or should the native reader clear each such line onto the build's cleared list? Keep both marked figures (5.03 and 5.27)? May 'Badhai ho!' and 'Congratulations.' go to Mummy and Mami? A Hindi-first reader checks 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', 'फ़ुल फ़िट', 'नो प्रॉब्लम', 'एकदम मिठाई', 'वेटिंग भी चलेगा' and 'Kursiyaan kam padin'; 🤗 is proposed as his and no other file claims it; every joke still waits on rulebook Q5.
